description: The case that discriminates a CORRECT implementation of this row from the obvious wrong one. "Lexical enclosure is therefore necessary but not sufficient: it must be enclosure by a `repeat` whose body the code runs as part of" (spec/execution-model.md:688-690). Line 1 has a `repeat` genuinely above the read in the AST, and is still an error — a handler invocation "is a separate, deferred instruction rather than part of the loop that registered it" (spec/execution-model.md:682-686). Line 2 is the mirror image and MUST stay clean: a `repeat` written inside the handler block "runs as part of the invocation", and the spec's own worked example says it prints 1, 2, 3 on each firing (spec/execution-model.md:686-688). A checker that asks only "is there a `repeat` above me" passes every other `repcount` fixture in the corpus and fails line 1; one that treats a handler block as unconditionally unenclosed fails line 2. Both are in one program so neither can be satisfied alone. Note what this fixture does NOT assert: measured, `execute()` on this exact program reports nothing and prints nothing, because neither handler is ever given a chance to fire — there is no `wait`. That is the runtime shape's own problem and `scoping/repcount-in-a-handler-has-no-enclosing-repeat` pins it, with the `wait` inside the loop body so the loop is still running when the handler fires. Here the semantic stage answers without needing the program to run at all. Line 3 is the third face of the same rule: a handler HEAD argument is not inside the handler block — it is an ordinary expression evaluated where the registration is written — so it reads the enclosing turn and stays clean (measured: `repeat 2 [ every repcount [ … ] ]` runs clean and schedules on the outer turn's number).
